sections.title: Today's Candidates (Momentum Scanner)
sections.intro: *What this part of the app is for:* Today's Candidates is a screener. Once per trading session, after the US close, the scanner checks every eligible US common stock against six fixed rules — the gates — and lists the ones that passed all six, split into a market bucket and a penny bucket. It narrows roughly five thousand stocks to a short, reviewable list of unusual moves on unusual volume. It does not rank them by how likely they are to keep going, and nothing on this page is a forecast.

entries.title: What this page claims — and does not

blocks.text: Every candidate on this page met the published gates. That is the whole claim: none of the columns, and not the score, has been shown to predict what happens next.

A gate is a pass/fail rule. A stock must pass **all six** gates on the session's closing data to appear on the list. Failing any one gate **excludes** it — it is not listed with a low score, it is not listed at all. Scoring only ever happens among stocks that have already passed.

Stocks are judged in one of two **buckets**, decided by closing **price**, not by company size: **market** (closing at $2.00 or more) and **penny** ($0.30 to $2.00). The two buckets use the same six gates with different thresholds. Stocks under $0.30 are not judged at all, because at those prices ticks and reverse splits dominate the numbers.

On a stock's detail page you can see a partial pass — for example "Failed 3 of 6 gates" — with each gate's actual value next to its threshold. That is how a stock that is not on today's list explains itself.

entries.title: The six gates, one by one

items: **Price** — market: at least $2.00; penny: $0.30 to $2.00. This is also what decides the bucket.
**History** — at least 252 daily bars (about a year of trading), so that the 52-week measures below always have a full window.

**Day change** — market: up +8% to +25% on the day; penny: up +10% to +40%. The upper bound is deliberate: the scanner is built to notice a move early, and a stock already up +60% today is past that point. The bound stops the list from filling with moves that have already happened.
**Relative volume (RVOL)** — market: at least 3.0× its usual volume; penny: at least 4.0×. A price move on ordinary volume is not what this screener looks for.

**Dollar volume** — market: at least $5 million traded; penny: at least $2 million. Without this, the penny bucket fills with stocks so thinly traded that a small order moves the price and the RVOL figure means little.
**Market cap** — market: $300 million to $10 billion; penny: $300 million or less. This is a size check inside the price-decided bucket; it does not change which bucket a stock is in.

blocks.text: All thresholds are published defaults of the scanner, and every one of them is applied to the session's closing data only.

**RVOL** is today's volume divided by the stock's average daily volume over the previous 20 sessions — today excluded, so an unusual day cannot inflate its own baseline. 3.0× means three times the usual volume. If fewer than 20 prior sessions exist, RVOL is blank and the stock fails the RVOL gate rather than being given a made-up value. The list is sorted by RVOL by default because it describes *how unusual* today was, which is what a screener is for — not because a higher RVOL has been shown to predict a better outcome (it has not; see Backtest Lab).

**Dollar volume** is the closing price times the day's share volume: roughly how much money changed hands in the stock that session. It is a liquidity check — a stock can have huge RVOL on a few thousand dollars of trading, and dollar volume is what screens that out.

**RSI(14)** is the standard 14-session Relative Strength Index (see MasterClass, Module 3, for what it is in general). On this list it is **not** a reason a stock scores higher. A stock breaking out on heavy volume is *expected* to show a high RSI, so rewarding RSI would reward exactly what every candidate already has, and rewarding a low RSI would select against the moves the screener is looking for. RSI is used only as a **penalty**: above 85, the score loses 5 points as "exhausted momentum". Otherwise it is shown for information.
**Breakout State** describes where today's close sits against the stock's highest high of the previous 20 sessions (today excluded), judged on the close, never on an intraday spike:

items: **breakout_from_consolidation** — closed above that 20-session high after a quiet stretch (the prior 20 sessions' range was under 25% of the price).
**breakout** — closed above that high without the quiet stretch before it.

blocks.text: What testing found

This field was tested for one question: does it help predict which candidates go on to rise **100% or more within 120 sessions**? In the original check on 218 candidates, the stocks in the stronger-breakout half reached +100% far *less* often than the weaker half (8 against 26 hits) — the field measured **inverted**. That is why its weight in the score was set to **zero**: it once earned up to 20 points, and now earns none.

A larger follow-up on 6,924 candidate episodes sharpened the picture instead of simply repeating it. **breakout_from_consolidation**, the most common state, reached +100% just 6.42% of the time, against 15.57% for **none**. But a plain **breakout** was the best state in that sample at 20.89%, above the 10.53% average. So "inverted" is true of the field as it was scored, and of its most common value — not of every value. One weight cannot fit both, which is a design finding, not a tuning one.

The likely reading is lateness: among stocks that have already passed the gates, a fresh breakout often marks a move further along, with less room left to run. Both checks were made on the scanner's earlier candidate definition and have not been repeated since. The field is still computed and shown because it describes the chart, and because it is informative in other ways — it simply does not add to the score.

**52-Week High %** is today's close divided by the highest high of the previous 251 sessions (today excluded). 100% means the stock closed exactly at its prior 52-week high; above 100% means today set a **new** 52-week high.
What testing found

Tested for the same question — reaching **+100% within 120 sessions** — it also measured **inverted**. In the original check on 218 candidates, the half nearer its 52-week high reached +100% less often (10 against 24 hits). In the 6,924-episode follow-up, candidates above the median reached +100% 6.70% of the time against 14.36% below it: a gap of 7.65 percentage points, far too large to be chance. Unlike Breakout State, this one held cleanly in both checks.

That is why its weight is **zero**. It once earned up to 5 points, the most of all for a fresh 52-week high — which is precisely the case that measured backwards. The reading is the same lateness: among stocks that have already passed the gates, being at a new high marks a move further along, not a better one. Both checks were made on the scanner's earlier candidate definition and have not been repeated since. The field is still computed and shown, because it describes where the price is.

**Catalyst Tier** is meant to say whether company news explains the move: **A** (strong news such as an approval, acquisition, major contract or raised guidance), **B** (weaker news such as an analyst upgrade or a partnership), or **none** (the stock was checked and there was no company news in the last 48 hours). A blank means the stock was **not checked** — and today that is every stock, because the news classifier is not yet running on live data. A blank is therefore missing information, not a sign that nothing happened; the detail page says "Not checked — catalyst data not yet ingested".

**Market Cap** is the value the market-cap gate uses: the session's closing price times the company's most recent share count **filed with the SEC** on or before that day. It is the same definition the scanner's research used, so today's list is drawn the same way as the history that was tested. If the company has no such filing, or its latest one is **more than 15 months old** — too old to trust once shares have been issued or reverse-split since — the market cap counts as unavailable and the stock fails the gate. The scanner never fills the gap with an estimate. Some companies that still file are excluded this way because their recent filings are missing from the scanner's data; that is a known gap, not a judgement about the company.

The **score** is a 0–100 research number computed only for stocks that passed the gates. It adds up weighted parts: relative volume (up to 35), volume acceleration (25), catalyst (15), estimated float (10), and trading above the 20-day volume-weighted average price (5). Breakout State and 52-Week High % are weighted **zero** because they measured inverted. Ten points are deliberately left unassigned, so the most any stock can reach is 90. Penalties then subtract points for exhausted momentum (RSI above 85), an already-extended day (up more than 20%), and volume that is high but already fading.

Each score is shown against **its own ceiling**, e.g. **53/75** rather than 53: the ceiling is 90 minus the weight of every part that is missing for that stock. With the catalyst part blank for every stock today, the ceiling is 75. Showing "/75" stops a 53 from reading as "53 out of 100".
The score is always labelled **unvalidated**, everywhere it appears:

The header reads, for example, "4,967 of 5,000 symbols scanned". **Eligible** is the list of stocks the scanner is meant to cover: common stock on NASDAQ, NYSE or NYSE American — no ETFs, funds, warrants, units, preferred shares, ADRs or REITs. **Scanned** is how many of them actually got a result for this session. The two differ when a stock's data is not available for that day — for example a missing daily bar — so it could not be evaluated. A stock that was not scanned is simply absent; it has not been judged and failed.

entries.title: Scan date and a stale scan

blocks.text: The **scan date** is the trading session the list covers. The scanner runs after the close, so each morning the list shows the previous session. The scan is **stale** when a newer session should exist by now — its 4:00 pm New York close plus a six-hour grace period has passed, on the NYSE's own trading calendar with its holidays — but no scan for it has been stored. Weekends and market holidays never make it stale. When it is stale, the page keeps showing the older, still-correct list and says so above it: "Couldn't load today's results — showing the scan from …".

Every column can be sorted, the score included, and the list opens sorted by RVOL. The sort line always says what it is — "Sorted by RVOL — descriptive, not predictive" — because reordering a list is not the same as ranking candidates by how good they are. That is why the "unvalidated" label stays next to the score in every row and every sort order: sorting by score puts the highest numbers on top, but those numbers have not been shown to predict anything, so the top of that list is not "the best" candidates.

sections.title: Stock Detail — full analysis
sections.intro: *What this part of the app is for:* Stock Detail is the full picture of one symbol. For a symbol the scanner covers, the top of the page shows which of the scanner's gates it passed or failed, its primary facts, and its score, marked unvalidated; a symbol the scanner has never covered shows "No scanner data for this symbol" there instead, and everything below still works. Below that comes the full analysis — technical readings, fundamentals, balance sheet, correlations, news, qualitative signals, and context against the market benchmark (SPY) — each a plain, neutral reading of stored data, not a signal. The first time a symbol's analysis is opened it may take a few seconds to compute, and the page says so instead of showing a spinner. Last comes Classical Technical Signals, the one section with its own accent colour, because it is pattern-matching rather than a reading of data; its entry below explains what it shows and what testing found.

blocks.text: *What this part of Stock Detail is for:* this is the one section that shows traditional technical-analysis signals — chart patterns, liquidity sweeps, order blocks, and a combined BUY_WATCH / TRIM_WATCH label. It has its own accent colour on purpose: everything above it is a plain reading of stored data; this section is pattern-matching, and it was tested.
What you see here

items: **Flagged readings** — technical readings that currently carry a severity (for example an active Bollinger squeeze, or RSI past its overbought/oversold threshold), repeated here from the technical grid so this section is the one place to see what is currently flagged.

**Chart patterns** — the pattern name, whether it is *confirmed* (for head & shoulders: the neckline has been broken; for triangles: price has broken out) or *unconfirmed*, and a severity badge. Flags have no confirmation step: detection is the signal.

**Action signal** — BUY_WATCH or TRIM_WATCH from the liquidity-sweep rule, with its reasoning lines and a confluence score out of 4 (sweep, close back across the swept level, an order block, the trend). Shown as plain "3/4", not a meter: it is a count of conditions, not a confidence level.

blocks.text: What testing found

Before any result was looked at, eleven hypotheses were written down, one per signal type. Each one tested whether the signal predicts a move of at least 3% in its claimed direction over the next 10 trading sessions. The test used about ten years of daily bars for 2,482 US stocks, and the bar for "meaningful" was fixed in advance.

items: **RSI oversold** (predicting a rise) was the only one to clear the bar on the main data, and only just (1.256 against a floor of 1.25). On the held-out period that had never been looked at, it fell to 1.153. That's below the floor, and statistically indistinguishable from no effect. **Not confirmed.**

**None of the other ten showed a meaningful effect.** RSI overbought was measurable but below the floor. MACD crosses, flags, head & shoulders and liquidity sweeps sat at or near no effect. A Bollinger squeeze was followed by slightly *smaller* moves, not larger ones.

**The BUY_WATCH / TRIM_WATCH labels** did no better than the best single signal. That result is about *this specific rule as built*, which has known weaknesses. It is not a verdict on combining signals in general.

blocks.text: Not tested
Triangles (ascending, descending, symmetrical) and double tops/bottoms appear in this section but were not part of the testing. The same caution applies to them, with no result behind it either way.
How to read this section

Everything here is still shown, exactly as built, because a visible, labelled null result is more useful than a hidden signal. Read it as a description of what the chart looks like, not as a forecast.
